title: Resonance
summary: Push a mass on a spring at its natural frequency, watch the response grow, and tame it with damping.

steps.title: Pushing near the natural frequency
steps.text:
This 1 kg mass on a 10 N/m spring has a natural frequency ωn = √(k/m) ≈ 3.16 rad/s. Here a force pushes it at ωf = 3 rad/s, close to ωn.

Load the setup and press Run. The Summary shows the magnification: how many times larger the steady swing is than the stretch the same force would cause if it were held steady.

check.hint: Load the setup, then press Run.
check.success: About 5.5: pushing near ωn already makes the swing several times larger.

steps.title: Hit resonance
steps.text: Set the forcing frequency ωf to match ωn, 3.16 rad/s, and run again. How large does the magnification get?

check.hint: Set Frequency ωf (in the Forcing section) to 3.16 rad/s.
check.success: With light damping, resonance multiplies the response by 1/(2ζ) ≈ 6.3.

steps.title: Damping tames resonance
steps.text:
Keep ωf at 3.16 rad/s and raise the damping c until the magnification falls below 2.

This is why car suspensions and tall buildings have dampers.

check.success: At resonance the magnification is 1/(2ζ), so more damping means a smaller peak.

steps.title: The whole response curve
steps.text: The Frequency response tab plots the magnification against ωf/ωn. To see the same thing in the time response, sweep the forcing frequency: the Analyze ▸ Sweep tab is set for ωf from 1 to 6 rad/s. Run it and plot "Peak displacement".
